senses.def: the state of lacking knowledge
senses.comment: For another interpretation of ἀγνωσία in 1 Corinthians 15:34, see 32.7. In 1 Peter 2:15, ἀγνωσία may involve lack of understanding (see 32.8).

senses.def: to not understand, with the implication of a lack of capacity or ability
senses.comment: It is also possible to interpret ἀγνωσία in 1 Corinthians 15:34 as meaning to not know about (see 28.16).

senses.def: that which is not understood or comprehended, implying a lack of capacity
senses.comment: For another interpretation of ἀγνωσία in 1 Peter 2:15, see 28.16.

senses.def: to assemble together, with the possible implication of compactness or solidarity
to become or to be ripe
senses.comment: In some languages the equivalent of ‘to ripen’ is ‘to become sweet’ or ‘to become edible.’

senses.def: white crystalline substance, mainly consisting of sodium chloride, used for seasoning or preserving food
senses.comment: Since salt is a universal condiment, there is no difficulty involved in finding an adequate expression for it, but there is a difficulty in Matthew 5:13, since pure salt cannot lose its taste. In the ancient world, however, what was often sold as salt was highly adulterated and the sodium chloride could leach out in humid weather, in which case the residue (normally a form of lime) would be useless. It may, therefore, be important in some languages to provide a marginal note explaining the basis for the biblical statement concerning salt losing its flavor; otherwise, the parable may appear to be either meaningless or misleading.

senses.subdomain: Duration of Time with Reference to Some Point of Time: Until, Delay, Still, From
senses.def: to extend a period of time by postponing an event
pertaining to a state of being maimed or mutilated, resulting in a crippling condition
to acknowledge one’s thankfulness, restricted in NT usage to contexts in which God is the one being thanked
pertaining to the absence of water or moisture
senses.comment: See also 1.86 for ἄνυδρος τόπος ‘lonely place.’|In the NT ἄνυδρος occurs in the figurative expressions ‘waterless springs’ (2 Peter 2:17) and ‘waterless clouds.’ A phrase such as ‘waterless springs’ may be rendered simply as ‘springs in which there is no water,’ but in some languages such a phrase would seem to be a complete contradiction, since a term for ‘spring’ would imply the existence of water. It may therefore be necessary to translate ‘waterless springs’ as ‘springs which have ceased to produce water.’ ‘Waterless clouds’ are often best rendered as ‘clouds which will not produce rain’ or ‘clouds from which no rain will fall.’ In Jude 1:12 the phrase ‘waterless clouds’ is a description of persons whose teaching and behavior are of no value in building up the faith of believers. Such a metaphor must often be changed into a simile, for example, ‘they are like clouds which do not produce rain.’

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: the quality of sincerity as an expression of singleness of purpose or motivation
an act of generosity
glosses: to act in a generous manner

senses.def: a king of Nabatean Arabia
to live in a manner contrary to proper religious beliefs and practice
glosses: to live in an ungodly manner

senses.def: a Latin title given to Emperor Octavian and equivalent to a proper name; ruled from 27 B.C. to 14 A.D.
pertaining to not being useful
senses.comment: In a number of languages usefulness or lack of usefulness can only be expressed in terms of a verb meaning ‘to help,’ so that in Philemon 1:11 it may be necessary to translate ‘at one time he did not help you at all and now he can help both you and me.’

senses.def: a name given to the Devil or to the Antichrist
the small round fruit, sweet and juicy, of a creeping plant that develops a woody stem when it matures; Vitis vinifera; symbol of blessing, prosperity, and happiness
senses.comment: Some scholars have contended that βότρυς means primarily a bunch of grapes, while σταφυλή designates individual grapes. In Revelation 14:18 this difference might seem plausible, but there is scarcely any evidence for such a distinction, since both words may signify grapes as well as bunches of grapes.|In some languages it is necessary to borrow a term for ‘grapes’ from a dominant language and then employ some kind of classifier, for example, ‘fruit called grapes.’ In other languages grapes may be known as ‘wine fruit,’ since wine may be more widely known than a term for grapes.

senses.domain: Groups and Classes of Persons and Members of Such Groups and Classes
senses.def: a person who lives close beside others and who thus by implication is a part of a so-called in-group, that is, the group with which an individual identifies both ethnically and culturally
senses.comment: It may be that of the three terms γείτων, περίοικος[b], the last is somewhat broader in meaning. At least πλησίον is used in Luke 10:27 in a somewhat extended sense of ‘fellow man,’ while ἀδελφός[e] probably suggests a more intimate or close relationship.

senses.def: to dress in worn-out, ragged clothing

senses.subdomain: Cloth, Leather, and Objects Made of Such Materials
senses.def: skin of an animal, normally including attached hair and sometimes tanned
senses.comment: In a number of languages it is important to distinguish clearly between tanned and untanned skins or hides. Furthermore, one must often make a distinction between a skin which still has the hair on it and that which does not. In Hebrews 11:37 the likelihood is that these skins were tanned and still retained the hair as extra protection.

senses.def: to cease from an activity which has gone on for some time
to provide instruction in a formal or informal setting
senses.comment: The equivalent of ‘to teach’ in many languages is simply a causative form of a verb meaning ‘to learn’ or ‘to know,’ for example, ‘to cause to learn’ or ‘to cause to know.’ In choosing a term for ‘to teach’ it is important to avoid an expression which will denote merely classroom activity.

senses.def: act of trying to learn the genuineness of something by examination and testing, often through actual use

senses.subdomain: Once, Twice, Three Times, Etc. [Cardinals of Time]
senses.def: seventy occurrences
senses.comment: For another interpretation of ἑβδομηκοντάκις in Matthew 18:22, see 60.77.

senses.subdomain: Double, Four Times As Much, Etc. [Multiples]
senses.def: seventy multiples of a quantity
senses.comment: One should not, however, interpret ἑβδομηκοντάκις ἑπτά as referring to a specific number, such as 490, but simply an unusually large number with symbolic significance of being totally adequate or complete. For another interpretation of ἑβδομηκοντάκις in Matthew 18:22, see 60.74.

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: to live in peace with others
senses.comment: In some languages the equivalent of ‘live in peace’ is a negation of fighting, for example, ‘do not fight’ or ‘do not constantly quarrel.’

senses.def: to carry or bring out, especially of a corpse for burial
to cause an object to move by means of a strong force or vigorous action
senses.comment: In Luke 8:29 ἐλαύνω occurs in the statement ἠλαύνετο ὑπὸ τοῦ δαιμονίου εἰς τὰς ἐρήμους ‘he was driven into the desert by the demon.’ In this context it would appear that the demon was regarded as a type of force, parallel perhaps to wind.

senses.def: to fall into a particular point or location
to experience somewhat suddenly that which is difficult or bad
to signal to someone by means of part of the body, especially by means of the head or hands
senses.comment: In a number of languages it is necessary to be quite specific with regard to types of gestures or motions of the head or hands and arms. For example, in John 13:24 there is an obvious question involved, and this may require in some languages a particular signal by means of the hands or face. The same would be true in the case of Luke 1:62. In Luke 1:22 the gesture would have to be something which would explain or indicate Zechariah’s inability to speak, while in Luke 5:7 quite another gesture would no doubt be called for, since the persons involved were at quite a distance from one another.

senses.def: to provide detailed information in a systematic manner
senses.comment: For another interpretation of ἐξηγέομαι in John 1:18, see 28.41.

senses.def: to make something fully known by careful explanation or by clear revelation
glosses: to make fully and clearly known
senses.comment: For another interpretation of ἐξηγέομαι in John 1:18, see 33.201.

senses.subdomain: To Think About, with the Implied Purpose of Responding Appropriately
senses.def: to take special notice of something, with the implication of concerning oneself
senses.comment: Though the terms ἐπιβλέπω, ἐπεῖδον (ἐφοράω), and ὁράω suggest as a result of their central meanings some measure of visual perception, what is involved in these specific contexts is much more than visual perception. The focus is actually upon intellectual activity and concern.

senses.def: to care for with diligent concern
to undertake to do something, but not necessarily without success

senses.subdomain: Definite Units of Time: Year, Month, Week, Day, Hour
senses.def: a unit of time involving a complete cycle of seasons
senses.comment: In a number of languages, years are described in terms of repeated seasons. For example, some languages would speak of ‘twelve years’ as being ‘twelve winters’ or ‘twelve summers,’ while in other languages one might have an expression such as ‘twelve rainy seasons’ or ‘twelve returns of the sun.’

senses.subdomain: Duration of Time without Reference to Points or Units of Time: Time, Spend Time, Always, Eternal, Old, Immediately, Young
senses.def: possibly a symbolic temporal expression denoting a very long period of time
senses.comment: Though most translations render ἔτη τεσσεράκοντα as ‘forty years,’ the expression probably is to be understood as meaning an unusually long period of time. See also discussion at 67.93.

senses.subdomain: A Point of Time with Reference to Other Points of Time: Before, Long Ago, Now, At the Same Time, When, About, After
senses.def: (an idiom, literally: through years) a point of time subsequent to another point of time after an interval of some years
pertaining to being affectionate and compassionate
leaven employed in making bread rise
senses.comment: In some languages yeast is described simply as ‘that which makes bread rise,’ but frequently yeast is described in terms of some characteristic or on the basis of its source, for example, ‘sour froth’ or ‘beer foam.’

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: (a figurative extension of meaning of ζύμη[a] ‘yeast,’ 5.11) hypocritical behavior, probably implying hidden attitudes and motivations
senses.comment: In Matthew 16:6 the ζύμη of the Pharisees and the Sadducees is equated with their teaching, but the context would indicate clearly that this was a type of hypocritical teaching, since the religious leaders said one thing but did something quite different.|In 1 Corinthians 5:6 there is an extended figurative reference to ζύμη. At first, ζύμη must be understood in the literal sense (as in Domain 5), yet ζύμη in verse 7 refers to wrong behavior. It is important, however, to try to preserve the continuity of the figurative reference, and for that reason the phrase παλαιὰ ζύμη is sometimes translated as ‘the old yeast of sin.’ It is difficult to know to what extent there may be a reference at this point to the hypocrisy which accompanies legalistic behavior.

senses.def: to bury a dead person
(possibly an idiom, literally: to bury my father) to take care of one’s father until his death
glosses: to take care of a father
to provide for one’s father until his death

senses.def: to weep or cry, especially in mourning for the dead
senses.comment: For another interpretation of θρηνέω in Luke 23:27, see 52.2.|Mourning and wailing for the dead are frequently expressed by a term very different from expressions employed in referring to events not involving death.

senses.def: to sing or chant expressions of mourning
to wail and lament for the dead, implying a ritualized form of mourning at funerals
senses.comment: For another interpretation of θρηνέω in Luke 23:27, see 25.141.

senses.def: the father of King David in the genealogy of Jesus
a person in the genealogy of Jesus
contraction of καὶ + ἐκεῖ
to cause injury or harm by means of a statement regarded as having some supernatural power, often because a deity or supernatural force has been evoked
the content of what is expressed in a curse
that which has been cursed
to see indirectly or by reflection as in a mirror
glosses: to see as in a mirror
senses.comment: The phrase ‘as in a mirror’ may be translated in some languages as ‘as though we were looking into a mirror’ or ‘as though what we saw was in a mirror.’ In some languages, however, one does not say ‘in a mirror’ but ‘through a mirror’ or ‘by means of a mirror.’ For another interpretation of κατοπτρίζομαι in 2 Corinthians 3:18, see 14.52.

senses.def: to reflect light or visual patterns coming from some source
senses.comment: In order to speak of a reflection of light, it may be necessary to say ‘to throw back the light’ or ‘to shine back the form.’ Sometimes it is necessary to stipulate a type of object which reflects such light, for example, ‘we are a shining object that shows back the glory of the Lord.’ For another interpretation of κατοπτρίζομαι in 2 Corinthians 3:18, see 24.44.

senses.def: a city in Phrygia in Asia Minor
a leader of the synagogue in Corinth
a Christian who sent greetings in 2 Timothy 4:21
the person elected to take the place of the apostle Judas Iscariot

senses.subdomain: High Status or Rank [including persons of high status]
senses.def: a state of greatness or importance
(a title for God, literally: majesty) one who is characterized by majesty and greatness
senses.comment: The use of ‘Majesty’ as a title for God may be rendered in some languages as ‘the one who is truly great’ or ‘… truly important.’ In other instances a more satisfactory equivalent is ‘the one who is truly wonderful.’

senses.def: to change one’s way of life as the result of a complete change of thought and attitude with regard to sin and righteousness
senses.comment: Though in English a focal component of repent is the sorrow or contrition that a person experiences because of sin, the emphasis in μετανοέω and μετάνοια seems to be more specifically the total change, both in thought and behavior, with respect to how one should both think and act. Whether the focus is upon attitude or behavior varies somewhat in different contexts. Compare, for example, Luke 3:8, Hebrews 6:1, and Acts 26:20.

senses.def: the name of the chief angel
a person in the genealogy of Jesus
pertaining to being correct according to rules and regulations

senses.subdomain: Groups and Members of Groups of Persons Regarded as Related by Blood but without Special Reference to Successive Generations
senses.def: (derivative of οἶκος[b] ‘family,’ 10.8) one who belongs to a particular household or extended family
the state of being similar to something
established or fixed boundaries

senses.domain: Body, Body Parts, and Body Products
senses.def: the front part of the human head
that which is thought to be true but is not necessarily so, since it is based upon mere appearance and external form
to indicate strongly to someone what he or she should plan to do
to maintain a state or condition
to cause something to happen to someone
senses.comment: In Luke 7:4, in some languages it may be more appropriate to translate ‘he deserves this favor from you’ or ‘he deserves your help.’ See also 90.91.

senses.def: to cause someone to experience something, with the possible implication of a duration
senses.comment: See also 13.127.

senses.def: a person who is poor and must live sparingly, but probably not as destitute as a person spoken of as πτωχός[a] (57.53)
a degree which is considerably in excess of some point on an implied or explicit scale of extent
to interlace strands, either by braiding or weaving
pertaining to being of great value or worth, implying in some contexts a monetary scale
the wife of Aquila
to give a name or title to

senses.subdomain: Acceptable To, To Be Pleased With
senses.def: pertaining to that which causes people to be pleased with something
to inquire about something
to acquire information by questioning
glosses: to find out about by inquiry
senses.comment: Since πυνθάνομαι[b] and διερωτάω imply quite distinct semantic components, namely ‘to acquire information’ and ‘by the process of questioning,’ it may be appropriate in many languages to use two verbs meaning ‘to ask’ and ‘to find out.’ Accordingly, this expression in Acts 10:17 may be rendered as ‘meanwhile, men sent by Cornelius asked and learned where Simon’s house was.’

senses.subdomain: Cause To Be Safe, Free from Danger
senses.def: to rescue from danger, with the implication that the danger in question is severe and acute
to express in attitude and ritual one’s allegiance to and regard for deity
senses.comment: In a number of languages worship is expressed in an idiomatic manner, for example, ‘to bow down before,’ ‘to lower one’s head before,’ ‘to raise one’s arms to,’ ‘to sing to,’ ‘to honor.’ It is important in selecting an expression for worship to employ a term or phrase which will include various aspects of worship.

senses.def: any kind of instrument, tool, weapon, equipment, container, or property
senses.comment: The manner in which σκεῦος[a] is translated depends in many instances upon the specific context. It may, of course, be rendered by a highly generic expression such as English ‘thing,’ but wherever the context refers to some particular type of object, it is preferable to employ a specific referent. In Acts 27:17, for example, the reference of σκεῦος is generally understood to be the mainsail.

senses.def: a highly generic term for any kind of jar, bowl, basket, or vase
senses.comment: In Acts 10:11 and Acts 10:16 σκεῦος[b] refers to a sheet (as a container) which was let down from heaven in Peter’s vision.|In a number of languages there is no relatively high generic term which may be used to refer to any type of vessel or container, and therefore one must employ more specific terms depending upon the context, even as in the case of most English translations in Acts 10:11, Revelation 2:27, and Luke 8:16.

senses.def: objects which are possessed
(a figurative extension of meaning of σκεῦος[a] ‘instrument, thing,’ 6.1) a person in relation to a particular function or role

senses.domain: Body, Body Parts, and Body Products
senses.def: (a figurative extension of meaning of σκεῦος[a] ‘object, thing, instrument,’ 6.1, or of σκεῦος[b] ‘vessel,’ 6.118) the human body
senses.comment: It is also possible to interpret σκεῦος in 1 Thessalonians 4:4 as meaning ‘wife,’ and for a discussion of this meaning and some of the problems involved in translation, see 10.55. A further alternative meaning, and one closely related to the meaning of ‘body’ is ‘sexual life,’ so that this expression in 1 Thessalonians 4:4 might be rendered as ‘each of you must gain mastery over his sexual life’ or, in the form τὸ ἑαυτοῦ σκεῦος κτᾶσθαι ἐν ἁγιασμῷ καὶ τιμῇ, ‘your sexual life should be holy and honorable’ (see 23.63).

senses.def: (a figurative extension of meaning of σκεῦος[b] ‘vessel,’ 6.118) a woman married to a man, with focus upon the sexual relation
senses.comment: The interpretation of σκεῦος in 1 Thessalonians 4:4 has given rise to serious divisions of opinion as noted in 8.6, where σκεῦος is interpreted as designating a person’s own body. The interpretation of σκεῦος as ‘wife’ is based upon a number of considerations. In the first place, the verb κτᾶσθαι ‘to get, to acquire’ (57.58) does not normally go with ‘body,’ while it fits well with the meaning of ‘wife.’ On the other hand, σκεῦος meaning ‘wife’ is nowhere else attested in Greek but is assumed in 1 Thessalonians 4:4 to refer to a wife primarily on the strength of the particular interpretation of the context, in which πορνεία ‘immorality’ (88.271) in verse 3 and and ἐν πάθει ἐπιθυμίας ‘with a lustful desire’ (25.30) in verse 5 are assumed to point to the meaning of σκεῦος as ‘wife.’ In ancient Jewish literature a wife was euphemistically called a ‘vessel’ in contexts relating to sexual relations, and ‘vessel’ is a very common meaning of σκεῦος in Greek. If, therefore, one assumes a Semitic background for this Greek text, the statement in 1 Thessalonians 4:4 would refer to the need for sexual life to be both holy and honorable (see 23.63).

senses.def: (an idiom, literally: to possess a vessel) a euphemistic manner of referring to sexual relations
senses.comment: It is also possible to understand σκεῦος in 1 Thessalonians 4:4 as one’s wife (see 10.55). σκεῦος in 1 Thessalonians 4:4 may also be understood as one’s body, and therefore the phrase τὸ ἑαυτοῦ σκεῦος κτᾶσθαι may be rendered as ‘to control his own body’ (see 8.6).

senses.domain: Body, Body Parts, and Body Products
senses.def: the inner parts of the body, especially the intestines
(figurative extension of meaning of σπλάγχνον[a] ‘intestines,’ 8.58) the psychological faculty of desire, intent, and feeling
senses.comment: Though some persons have attempted to distinguish between σπλάγχνον[b], κοιλία[c], and νεφρός, it is extremely doubtful whether this is really possible or practical. The semantic focus in the use of these terms is clearly the deeper and more intimate feelings and emotions. In some languages one can use a term which literally means ‘belly’ or ‘bowels,’ but more often than not, these emotions are associated with some particular organ of the body such as heart, spleen, liver, etc. Rather, however, than attempting to employ a figurative expression which may or may not be fully equivalent, it is often preferable to refer to the emotional content by using terms such as ‘feelings,’ ‘intents,’ ‘desires,’ or ‘compassion,’ depending upon the context.

senses.def: experiencing great affection and compassion for someone
senses.comment: In Philippians 1:8 the phrase ἐν σπλάγχνοις Χριστοῦ Ἰησοῦ is ambiguous. It may mean ‘because of the compassion which Christ Jesus himself has for you’ or ‘… for me.’ On the other hand, it may also be interpreted as characterizing the kind of love which Paul has for the believers, for example, ‘how I long for all of you, even with the kind of love Christ Jesus himself has for you.’

senses.def: one for whom there is deep affection or compassion
(an idiom, literally: to be restricted in the bowels) to restrict one’s affection for someone
glosses: to not respond with affection to someone
senses.comment: In 2 Corinthians 6:12 it is also possible to understand στενοχωρέομαι as meaning ‘to live with severe restrictions’ (see 37.18), and σπλάγχνα may be interpreted as a psychological faculty of intent and feeling (see 26.11).

senses.def: to distort the meaning of something in communicating to others

senses.subdomain: To Intend, To Purpose, To Plan
senses.def: to engage in joint planning so as to devise a course of common action, often one with a harmful or evil purpose

senses.domain: Groups and Classes of Persons and Members of Such Groups and Classes
senses.def: an advisory council
senses.comment: In Acts 25:12 it is possible to render ‘council’ as ‘those persons who gave him their opinions’ or ‘those who were his advisors’ or even ‘those who said what should be done’ or ‘… what was best to do.’

senses.def: to be in prison along with others
to pull or drag, requiring force because of the inertia of the object being dragged
to drag or pull by physical force, often implying resistance

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: the quality of unpretentious behavior, suggesting a total lack of arrogance or pride
senses.comment: In some languages humility is expressed indirectly by an idiomatic phrase, for example, ‘to live without strutting’ or ‘to walk without wanting to be noticed.’

senses.subdomain: Low Status or Rank [including persons of low status]
senses.def: the state of low status, with the probable implication of humility
a city on the west shore of the Lake of Galilee
the Lake of Tiberias, also known as the Lake of Galilee
to put up with someone or something, implying extensive patience
to submit to the orders or directives of someone
a piece of furniture on which one may rest one’s feet
senses.comment: Since footstools are a common cultural feature in many parts of the world, it is rarely necessary to use a descriptive phrase. One can, however, use an expression such as ‘a thing on which to rest one’s feet.’ In some languages the functional equivalent of a footstool is a ‘footstick,’ that is to say, a stick on which one normally places the feet in order to raise them from the relatively damp dirt floor of a typical house or hut.

senses.def: (an idiom, literally: footstool of the feet) to be under the complete control of someone
senses.comment: In a number of languages it is simply not possible to preserve the idiom ‘under the feet of,’ though in some instances one may use a parallel idiom, for example, ‘to stand on,’ so that 1 Corinthians 15:25 might be rendered ‘until he stands on all his enemies,’ but it is more likely that the idiom in this context is better rendered as ‘until he defeats all his enemies.’

senses.def: to speak, with focus upon verbal sound rather than upon content
to beat severely with a whip

senses.subdomain: Pattern, Model, Example, and Corresponding Representation
senses.def: a representation as an exact reproduction of a particular form or structure

senses.subdomain: Assign to a Role or Function
senses.def: (figurative extension of meaning of χρίω ‘to anoint,’ not occurring in the NT) to assign a person to a task, with the implication of supernatural sanctions, blessing, and endowment
senses.comment: It is rare that one can employ a literal rendering of χρίω or χρῖσμα in such contexts as Luke 4:18 and 1 John 2:20, since ‘to pour oil upon someone’ as a means of conveying a supernatural blessing and endowment for a task is culturally very rare. A strictly literal rendering of χρίω or χρῖσμα as ‘to pour oil upon’ is likely to be interpreted either as an insult or as an event preparatory to setting a person on fire and thus to destroy or to torture. Accordingly, in place of a literal rendering of χρίω or χρῖσμα, it is often necessary to employ some such expression as ‘to be appointed by God’ or ‘to be given a special task by God.’

senses.def: (an Aramaic expression meaning ‘help, I pray’ or ‘save, I pray,’ but which had become a strictly liturgical formula of praise) a shout of praise or adoration
senses.comment: In Matthew 21:9 ὡσαννὰ τῷ υἱῷ Δαυίδ may also be rendered as ‘praise to you, Son of David’ or ‘we praise you who are the Son of David’ or ‘… a descendant of David.’|Though for many early Christians, and especially those of Jewish background, ὡσαννά would be known from its Aramaic background as meaning ‘help’ or ‘save,’ nevertheless, its association with liturgical expressions involving praise and exaltation resulted in the expression acquiring quite a different significance; hence, a phrase such as ‘hosanna in the highest’ became equivalent to ‘praise be to God.’ For growing numbers of Christians without Jewish background, ὡσαννά probably acquired much the same meaning as it now has in English.
